extract:
Maná is a Mexican rock band from Guadalajara, Jalisco, and one of the most commercially successful acts in Spanish-language rock. The group's roots go back to the late 1970s and early 1980s, and it has been active under the Maná name since the mid-1980s. Over the following decades it grew from a local Guadalajara band into a stadium-filling act with a pan-American audience, combining rock en español with pop balladry and Latin rhythms.

The band began as Sombrero Verde, a Guadalajara group built around brothers Juan Diego, Ulises and Juan Calleros alongside singer Fernando "Fher" Olvera. Sombrero Verde released material in the early 1980s but struggled in a Mexican market that was largely unwelcoming to homegrown rock. Drummer Alex González, who would become Olvera's main creative partner, joined during this period. The lineup later reorganized and adopted the name Maná, drawing on the Police, reggae, and the Latin American rock movement that was emerging in Mexico, Argentina and Spain. They released a self-titled debut in 1987.

The breakthrough came with Falta Amor in 1990, their first album for Warner's Latin division, which yielded the hit "Rayando el Sol." Its follow-up, ¿Dónde Jugarán Los Niños? (1992), became a landmark of Latin rock and one of the best-selling Spanish-language rock albums of its era. It produced a run of standards: "Oye Mi Amor," "Vivir Sin Aire," "Te Lloré un Río" and "¿Dónde Jugarán los Niños?" The live set En Vivo (1994) captured the band's growing arena presence. Cuando Los Ángeles Lloran (1995) sharpened the band's environmental themes, with its title track dedicated to the murdered Brazilian activist Chico Mendes. Guitarist Sergio Vallín joined around this time. Sueños Líquidos (1997) brought hits such as "Clavado en Un Bar" and "En El Muelle De San Blas" and won a Grammy Award.

In 1999 the band recorded MTV Unplugged, an acoustic reinterpretation of its catalog that reinforced its reputation as a live act. That same year Maná appeared with Carlos Santana on "Corazón Espinado" from Santana's multi-platinum Supernatural. Santana returned the favor on Revolución De Amor (2002), which featured the hit "Ánimal Nocturno." The band's commitment to activism led to the creation of the Selva Negra foundation, which supports environmental causes, a connection referenced in the release pairing "En El Muelle De San Blas" with "Selva Negra." Later studio albums included Amar es Combatir (2006), Drama y Luz (2011) and Cama Incendiada (2015).

Critics and the industry have consistently recognized Maná as a defining band of rock en español. They have won multiple Grammy and Latin Grammy awards, and Olvera and González's songwriting has become part of the standard Latin American popular songbook. Their touring record is equally notable: the band set attendance records at Los Angeles' Forum, where an extended residency led the venue to temporarily rename itself in their honor. Their popularity among Latino audiences in the United States has made them one of the most important crossover touring acts in Latin music.

Maná remains active as a touring band anchored by Olvera, González, Calleros and Vallín. Its catalog has been reissued in remastered editions, and in 2024 the band was nominated for the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, a rare honor for a Spanish-language group. Its legacy rests on proving that Mexican rock could achieve arena-level success without abandoning Spanish-language songwriting or its social and environmental commitments.
title: Maná
